one_liner: Clipper1: two-file C++ Vatti polygon clipper and offsetter on integer coordinates; reported faster than Boost.Geometry on simple Booleans.
what_it_does: Clipper (now called Clipper1) performs intersection, union, difference and XOR on closed polygons and open polylines, plus polygon and line offsetting (ClipperOffset) and Minkowski sums. It accepts self-intersecting input and four fill rules (EvenOdd, NonZero, Positive, Negative). The API is its own, not Boost.Geometry's: you add subject and clip Paths (std::vector of IntPoint) to a Clipper object and call Execute(ClipType, solution, fill types), getting either flat Paths or a PolyTree with hole nesting. Coordinates are integers, so floating-point data must be scaled in and out.
how_it_is_fast: It implements Bala Vatti's scanline clipping algorithm: local minima are sorted once, a std::priority_queue of scanbeam Y values drives the sweep, and an active edge list is updated per scanbeam, with crossings found by bubble-sorting the active edges at the top of each beam. All coordinates are integers (64-bit by default), and 128-bit multiplication (an internal Int128 class) is used only when a coordinate exceeds +/-0x3FFFFFFF, so most inputs run on plain 64-bit math. The docs quote about 10% more speed for flat Paths output instead of PolyTree and 20-30% for the use_int32 build.
when_to_use: Legacy C++ code (or C#/Delphi) already on ClipperLib 6.x, especially via the many third-party ports bundled in the zip (Python, Java, Go, Ruby, Lua, Matlab and others), where switching APIs is not worth it.

Polygon Booleans with few edge crossings per scanline, such as clipping to tiles or windows and unioning modest shape sets, the case where the third-party wrapper benchmark had Clipper ahead of Boost.Geometry.
Offsetting closed or open paths with square, round or miter joins and butt, square or round ends, using integer-scaled CAD, CNC, PCB or 2D game geometry.
Projects that want a BSL-1.0 two-file source drop (clipper.hpp + clipper.cpp) with no dependencies beyond the C++ standard library.
when_not_to_use: New code: the SourceForge page marks Clipper1 obsolete and unmaintained, superseded by Clipper2 (same author, BSL-1.0); among catalogued siblings, clipper2next reports about 1.6x over Clipper2 on intersection and union.

Inputs with many intersections, or long multi-stage tests: the same snippet-only benchmark says Boost.Geometry was fastest in a longer test and Boost.Geometry and GEOS scale better as intersection counts grow. The per-scanbeam bubble sort over active edges is consistent with that.
Floating-point workflows that cannot accept snapping to an integer grid: rounding can leave tiny self-intersection artefacts that need CleanPolygons or StrictlySimple.
You need validity repair, spatial predicates, buffering on a sphere or OGC semantics: it only clips and offsets planar paths; GEOS-class work fits qdgeo or GeoRepair better.
You need a reproducible speed claim: no benchmark with numbers, compiler or hardware could be opened, so the evidence is tier D.

integration.min_toolchain: C++98-era code; CMake 2.6 build script (shared library by default, SOVERSION 22)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; all sweep state lives in each Clipper/ClipperOffset object (no static mutable state seen in clipper.cpp), so one object per thread is the safe assumption

gotchas: Coordinate limits in the 6.4.2 code differ from the docs: the fast range is +/-0x3FFFFFFF and the hard limit +/-0x3FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF (about 4.6e18); with use_int32 the code limit is +/-0x7FFF (32,767), stricter than the documented +/-46,340. Out-of-range points make AddPath throw clipperException.
Errors are reported by throwing clipperException (derived from std::exception), including internal errors such as 'ProcessIntersections error' and 'DoMaxima error'.
Open paths must be added as subjects and need PolyTree output for line clipping; adding them as clip paths throws.
The 6.x API renamed Polygon/Polygons to Path/Paths and replaced OffsetPolygons with ClipperOffset, so older 4.x/5.x snippets and benchmarks (the third-party one used 5.1.2) do not compile unchanged.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Clipper1 only when you are tied to its API or one of its language ports; for new work, Clipper2 or clipper2next are the maintained successors, and CavalierContours is faster for arc-aware offsetting (3.5x to 4x on its square and pathological profiles, though slower on others).
verified_claims_summary: The only comparison is a third-party .NET-wrapper benchmark of nine C/C++ clipping libraries (Clipper 5.1.2, Boost 1.53, GEOS 3.3.7, among others), seen only through search snippets: Clipper was fastest in one test, followed by Boost.Geometry, but Boost.Geometry won a longer test and scaled better with more intersections. No numbers, compiler, flags or hardware were visible, and every timing includes .NET marshalling.
status_note: Abandoned: last release 6.4.2 (27 Feb 2017, changelog and header date), marked obsolete in favour of Clipper2, but BSL-1.0, dependency-free and about 5,000 lines, so it is easy to vendor and still downloaded about 7,300 times a week.
